examples: I have to submit the report by today.
The team lead told me to rewrite the report.
I worked late writing the weekly report.
nuance: 보고서 is the standard word for a written work report, from a quick 주간 보고서 (weekly report) to a big project one. Use 작성하다 in formal or email contexts and the plainer 쓰다 when chatting with coworkers.
mistakes: Saying 보고서를 만들다, which sounds like physically crafting an object
Confusing 보고서 (document) with 발표 (the spoken presentation)

usage: to be pressed by a deadline
examples: The deadline is tomorrow so I'm super busy.
This time I'll definitely meet the deadline.
Chased by the deadline, I couldn't even eat lunch.
nuance: 마감 covers any closing point: a report due date, an application cutoff, or even a shop's last order. The idiom 마감에 쫓기다 (chased by the deadline) is how Koreans describe last-minute crunch.
mistakes: Using English-style 데드라인 in formal writing instead of 마감
Saying 마감을 만나다 (literal 'meet') instead of the correct 마감을 지키다

examples: 부장님 결재를 받아야 진행할 수 있어요.
I can only proceed after the manager's sign-off.
I just submitted it for approval, please check.
아직 결재가 안 나서 기다리는 중이에요.
The approval hasn't come through yet, so I'm waiting.
nuance: 결재 is the formal sign-off a superior gives on documents or spending, usually now done in groupware (전자결재). Note the spelling: 결재 (approval) is different from the look-alike 결제 (payment), which Koreans constantly mix up.
mistakes: Spelling it 결제, which actually means paying money
Saying 결재를 하다 about yourself when you're the one requesting it; you 결재를 받다

examples: I have a client meeting this afternoon, so I'm out of office.
nuance: 거래처 means a company you do business with: a client, vendor, or supplier depending on context. The slangy 거래처를 뚫다 (literally 'break through') is how salespeople proudly say they won a new account.
mistakes: Using 손님 (customer) for a B2B partner instead of 거래처
Calling an individual person a 거래처; it refers to the company or account

examples: Sales went up a lot this month.
During COVID sales dropped by half.
I'm stressed because I can't hit the sales target.
nuance: 매출 is top-line sales/revenue, the total money coming in before costs, distinct from 수익/이익 (profit). It pairs with 오르다/떨어지다 for going up or down, and 매출 목표 (sales target) is a constant phrase in any sales team.
mistakes: Confusing 매출 (revenue) with 이익 or 수익 (profit after costs)
Saying 매출이 많다 when you mean 매출이 높다 for a high figure

examples: I work in the marketing department.
Next month I'm transferring to another department.
nuance: 부서 is the general word for a department or division within a company, while a smaller working unit is a 팀 (team). Newcomers hear 어느 부서예요? constantly when introducing themselves, so it's worth having ready.
mistakes: Mixing up 부서 (department) with 부장 (the department head, a person)
Treating 부서 and 팀 as identical; a 팀 is usually a smaller unit inside a 부서

usage: to report to the team lead
examples: The team lead is in a meeting right now.
I got promoted to team lead this time.
I have to report to the team lead first.
nuance: 팀장 is the team leader, your most immediate boss in many Korean companies, and you almost always add 님 when speaking to or about them. Ranks climb from 팀장 up through 부장, 이사, and 대표, so knowing 팀장 anchors the rest.
mistakes: Dropping the honorific 님 when addressing your boss directly
Calling them 팀장씨; 씨 is too casual for someone above you

examples: I attached the report to the email.
Oops, I forgot to attach the file.
nuance: 첨부 means attaching a file, and 첨부 파일 (attached file) is one of the most-used phrases in Korean work email. The line 첨부 파일을 확인해 주세요 (please check the attachment) is near-mandatory email etiquette.
mistakes: Saying 붙이다 (physically stick) for files instead of 첨부하다
Writing 첨부파일 as one word in formal mail; 첨부 파일 is the standard spacing

usage: to go out on field work
to be out on field work
to have a lot of field work
examples: I'm on field work this afternoon, so I'm away from my desk.
Mr. Kim is out in the field right now.
I'm in sales, so I have a ton of field work.
nuance: 외근 means working outside the office, like visiting clients or sites, the opposite of 내근 (desk/in-office work). Saying 외근 중이에요 is a tidy way to explain why a coworker isn't at their seat.
mistakes: Confusing 외근 (off-site work) with 출장 (an overnight business trip)
Saying 외근 가다 for going home; it specifically means leaving for work duties

examples: Our company allows working from home.
Today is a WFH day, so I'm working at home.
Since I work from home, commuting got easier.
nuance: 재택근무 is the formal term for working from home, often shortened to 재택 in casual speech (오늘 재택이에요). It surged after COVID, so asking 재택근무 가능해요? is a normal question when job hunting.
mistakes: Saying 집에서 근무 as a fixed term; the set word is 재택근무
Confusing it with 외근, which means going OUT for work, not staying home

examples: I work late every day these days because of a project.
If I work late, do I get overtime pay?
오늘은 야근 안 하고 칼퇴할 거예요.
Today I won't work late; I'm leaving right on time.
nuance: 야근 specifically means staying late at the office at night, the classic symbol of Korean work culture. Its natural opposite in slang is 칼퇴 (leaving exactly at quitting time), and 야근 수당 (overtime pay) is what everyone wants for it.
mistakes: Using 야근 for general overtime; daytime/holiday extra work is 특근 or 추가 근무
Saying 야근을 가다 instead of 야근을 하다

examples: I'll take a leave day next Friday.
I still have 5 days of leave left this year.
I took leave and went on a trip.
nuance: 연차 is your annual paid vacation entitlement, counted in days, and 연차를 쓰다 (use a leave day) or 연차를 내다 (file for leave) are the everyday phrases. A half day off is 반차, a handy related word for slipping out early.
mistakes: Confusing 연차 (paid leave) with 휴가, which is the broader 'vacation/leave' word
Saying 연차를 하다 instead of 연차를 쓰다 or 연차를 내다
